title: Knowledge Check 9: Lessons 65-72
description: Questions pooled from Lessons 65-72 of the agentic-ai series. Score 80% or higher to progress toward the practice exam.

questions.question: A team wants to fine-tune an agent to write support replies in a warm tone and a fixed closing format. Which dataset approach matches the lesson's guidance?
options: Scrape every historical support thread available, because more data is always better for training a tone skill.
Assemble roughly seventy realistic prompt-and-output pairs from real cases with manually reviewed ground truth, formatted as JSONL chat messages, keeping a held-out set out of training.
Generate all examples with a weaker model so they are uniform, and feed them all into the training run without any held-out set.
Start with less than ten examples and rely on more epochs to make up the difference.
questions.explanation: The lesson cites OpenAI's guidance that improvements begin around fifty to one hundred examples and that fifty well-crafted demonstrations is the recommended start, with human ground truth where the behavior is subtle. The data is formatted as JSONL chat messages, and a held-out set must be carved out and kept out of training so evaluation stays honest. More data is not automatically better, and a weaker model written set without a held-out ruler would make the change unmeasurable.

questions.question: How does LoRA make adapting a large model affordable compared with full fine-tuning?
options: It pre-computes all weight updates ahead of time so no gradient calculation happens during training.

It freezes the base model and trains a small set of low-rank update matrices A and B, dropping GPT-3-scale trainable parameters from billions to about 18 million and cutting GPU memory by roughly two thirds.
It shrinks the training dataset by selecting only the highest-loss examples.
It replaces the base model with a much smaller model that requires no training at all.
questions.explanation: LoRA keeps the original weight matrix W frozen and represents the adaptation as the product of two smaller matrices, so the adapted weight becomes W plus B times A. Because those small matrices hold far fewer parameters, trainable parameters collapse, with the IBM reference putting GPT-3 full fine-tuning at about 175 billion versus roughly 18 million under LoRA and GPU memory reduced by about two thirds. The rank r is a tunable hyperparameter where a lower rank means fewer trainable parameters but can cost accuracy.

questions.question: During a fine-tuning run, a team sees training loss keep falling while validation loss starts rising, and they are tempted to call the job a success because training looks great. The lesson says what?
options: This is the overfitting signal: the model is memorizing the training examples instead of learning a transferable behavior, and they should inspect the failing validation examples rather than ship the model on training loss alone.
Rising validation loss is normal and self-corrects, so they should wait for it to fall again before deciding.
Training loss is the only trustworthy metric, so the model is ready for production.
They should delete the validation data so the loss curves no longer diverge.
questions.explanation: The lesson repeats the Microsoft guidance that if training loss falls while validation loss rises, the model is overfitting, and the right move is to inspect the failing validation examples. It also stresses the OpenAI sequence of setting up evaluation first and comparing the tuned model against the base model on an immutable held-out set, so a model that only does well on training data should not be trusted. Deleting validation data would be data manipulation, not a fix.

questions.question: Per lesson 66, what is the actual mechanism a multimodal agent uses to let the word "the red car" bind to the red pixels in an image?
options: It runs a separate OCR step before the text model sees anything
Cross-attention, where the projected text features selectively focus on relevant parts of the projected image features inside the shared embedding space
It converts the image into a text description first and then embeds that description as normal text
The vision transformer replaces the language model entirely so text and image never need to combine
questions.explanation: The lesson explains fusion as the stage where the model combines projected features into a unified representation, and identifies cross-attention as the mechanism that lets one modality selectively focus on relevant parts of another, which is how a descriptive word binds to the corresponding image content.

questions.question: An agent must read the total off a clean, large-print receipt and approve it under a threshold. Following the lesson, what is the correct perception budget and routing?
options: High detail always, because any image an agent processes must be seen at maximum resolution
Low-detail vision, because reading a number from a clean image does not justify paying tile tokens for every 512-pixel square
A specialized table-structure extraction pipeline, because vision models always hallucinate amounts
No vision at all, since receipts can be reliably transcribed from the email text alone
questions.explanation: The lesson notes that with low detail an image costs only base tokens regardless of dimensions, and the worked example uses low-detail vision for a clean large-print receipt, reserving a table-structure extractor for dense or tabular receipts.

questions.question: For a dense, tabular PDF where every table cell must be reproduced exactly for downstream processing, what does the NVIDIA experiment in lesson 66 show about a general vision-language model versus a specialized extraction pipeline?
options: The general model is faster and more accurate, so it should always be used for tables
The specialized pipeline wins on both accuracy (higher recall@5) and speed, while the general model misread chart elements, missed embedded text, and hallucinated details
Both approaches are equally accurate, so the choice is purely cosmetic
The general model is more accurate but the pipeline is faster, so accuracy should win
questions.explanation: The lesson cites the NVIDIA PDF extraction comparison in which the specialized multistage pipeline beat the 11B vision-language model by 7.2 percent recall@5 and processed pages about 32 times faster, and the error analysis showed the general model misinterpreting elements and hallucinating.

questions.question: Per lesson 67, why does the three-piece STT to LLM to TTS pipeline dominate production voice agents even though realtime speech-to-speech models exist?
options: Because speech-to-speech models are always more expensive, so the pipeline is the only affordable option
Because the LLM wants text, and the voice components translate audio into that token space and back, while measured open speech-to-speech models are still too slow for realtime interaction
Because the pipeline is the only architecture that supports any form of streaming
Because speech-to-speech models cannot produce natural prosody, so the pipeline is the only natural-sounding choice
questions.explanation: The lesson frames a voice agent as an LLM agent with voice I/O: the reasoning and tool use happen in the LLM's token space, which wants text, and the voice components translate audio in and out. It also cites the Salesforce measurement that Qwen2.5-Omni, a representative open speech-to-speech model, was too slow for realtime interaction at roughly 13 seconds of time-to-first-audio.

questions.question: A voice agent feels slow even though its LLM is fast. Following the lesson, what is the most likely cause and the correct fix?
options: The LLM is too small, so the fix is to use a larger model
The stages run sequentially instead of overlapping, so the fix is to stream partial transcripts into the LLM and stream partial text into TTS so nothing waits for a stage to fully finish
The TTS voice quality is too low, so the fix is to upgrade the voice
The STT model is too accurate, so the fix is to use a faster but less accurate one
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that the latency budget only closes when stages overlap: recognition emits words while the user is still speaking, the decision model is primed on the partial transcript, and streaming TTS speaks the first clause while the model generates the rest. A fast model alone does not fix a sluggish agent if endpointing or non-streaming synthesis keeps it slow.

questions.question: A caller says "yeah" while the agent is reading a long explanation, and the agent stops talking and treats it as a new request. Per lesson 67, what went wrong?
options: The agent's barge-in policy failed to classify the input as a backchannel, which should not cancel critical audio
The agent's echo cancellation was too aggressive and removed the caller's speech
The agent's STT model had too high a word error rate on the word "yeah"
The agent's turn detection was set to model-based, which is always wrong for short inputs
questions.explanation: The lesson treats barge-in as a policy, not a toggle, and classifies each input: a caller saying "yeah" while listening is a backchannel that should usually not interrupt, while a true correction like "no, I meant Friday" should. A false barge-in that stops for a backchannel is more damaging than a missed one.

questions.question: Per lesson 68, what is the single structural fact that makes computer-use safety possible?
options: The model returns a proposed gesture, and a control layer your code owns performs it, so guardrails can sit between the model's idea and the real world
Computer-use agents never contact external websites, so there is nothing for an attacker to inject
The model executes every mouse and keyboard action directly, so there is no intermediary
The accessibility tree is always available, so the agent never has to trust page content
questions.explanation: The lesson stresses the separation: the model never touches the mouse directly, it returns a proposal, and a control layer you wrote decides whether to carry it out. That separation is what lets you place guardrails between the model and the real world, and it is called the most important architectural fact of the category.

questions.question: A computer-use agent keeps misclicking on a dense, JavaScript-heavy portal even though it reads the page structure perfectly. Following the lesson, which improvement is most directly supported?
options: Switch to a hybrid approach that falls back to screenshots when the structured signal runs out, since noisy DOMs are where structured-only agents lose out
Remove the step cap so the agent can keep trying until it succeeds
Widen the origin allowlist to give the agent more page access
Disable the human approval gate so the loop runs faster
questions.explanation: The lesson explains the hybrid approach: default to the cheap structured signal (accessibility tree or DOM) and fall back to screenshots when the structure runs out, because on navigation-heavy, JavaScript-heavy sites where the DOM gets messy, structured-only agents fall behind. A benchmark cited in the lesson showed a vision agent scoring roughly half again better than a text-only tree reader.

questions.question: An invoice page contains hidden text that tells the agent to change a payment beneficiary. Following the lesson, why is the guardrail stack expected to stop this even if the model absorbs the instruction?
options: Because the model reads page content as untrusted and never imports it into its reasoning

Because an allowlist restricts the agent to its one origin and removes the email tool, while a human approval gate stands before the anti-redundant high-value payment action, so the instruction cannot cascade into an action
Because prompt injection can only redirect the agent's answer, never its actions
Because vision model image downscaling drops all hidden text before the model sees it
questions.explanation: In the worked example, the agent reads the injected note but the guardrails hold: the instruction set tells it the user's conversation instructions outrank on-screen content, the allowlist gives it no email tool or other origin to extend to, and the payment is above the approval threshold so the loop pauses for a human who checks the trace. Consequential paths run through controls a person or code owns, so a successful injection does not produce an action.

questions.question: Per lesson 69, what is the single most useful reframe of the build-versus-buy decision for agents?
options: Treat it as a choice of where to permanently park your orchestration layer, buying the commodity layers and building the domain logic that is your product
Always build every layer yourself, because any framework or platform is a dependency you cannot audit
Always rent a managed platform, because speed of shipping is the only thing that matters
Choose whichever path shows the lowest initial setup cost, since exit cost is never knowable in advance
questions.explanation: The lesson reframes the question: the build-versus-buy argument is not build the whole stack versus rent the whole stack. It is buy the things that are commodities, build the thing that is your product, and choose your orchestration layer deliberately. Domain logic is the one layer where building is consistently justified, because it is what competitors cannot replicate.

questions.question: An Adroit invoice agent must read financial data and apply proprietary anomaly rules. Following the worked example's reasoning, which path does the lesson support and why?
options: An open-source framework like LangGraph, because it runs on your own infrastructure, lets you mix deterministic domain steps with model-driven steps, and keeps the vendor from owning the orchestration of regulated data
A managed platform, because its built-in oracle text is never the bottleneck and it is the fastest route to a demo
Build every wall from primitives, because writing your own router entirely eliminates all retraining and maintenance cost
An open-source framework, because it guarantees you never need to maintain the runtime or implement any orchestration
questions.explanation: Adroit chose an open-source framework because the rules, compliance checks, and approval thresholds are proprietary and auditors need deterministic steps readable in a diff; durable Linux-foundation-governed state and hand-coded domain nodes keep the vendor out of the orchestration of financial data. Building from primitives was rejected because it would mean maintaining a bespoke loop, and the platform was rejected on governance grounds.

questions.question: Following lesson 69, what is the strongest escape hatch for reducing the cost of switching agent frameworks or model vendors later?
options: Expose your tool integrations and data access as MCP servers, a vendor-neutral open standard now governed under the Linux Foundation, so those connections stay portable across orchestration paths
Store all agent state in a proprietary platform-specific format so it is optimized for your current runtime
Hard-code each tool call directly into your agent code with no shared interface, as there is no way to change frameworks predictably
Rely on a single vendor's ecosystem for both orchestration and data access so you get the tightest possible integration
questions.explanation: The lesson calls MCP the single most effective hedge against lock-in: exposing a capability once as an MCP server lets any compatible application use it, collapsing the integration matrix from N times M to N plus M. Because MCP was donated to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation and is adopted across major vendors, your tool connections survive a framework or model change.

questions.question: Per lesson 70, what is the architectural question that separates a workflow from an agent?
options: How capable the underlying model is, since stronger models enable agents and weaker ones are limited to workflows
Who owns the decision of what happens next: in a workflow your code fixes the path, while in an agent the model dynamically directs its own process and tool use
Whether the system runs on a single server or across a cluster
Whether the prompt uses tools or not, since an agent is simply any system that calls an API
questions.explanation: The lesson says the distinction is not about model capability; both use the same model. It is about who owns the decision of what happens next. A workflow orchestrates LLMs and tools through predefined code paths, while an agent lets the LLM dynamically direct its own processes and tool usage, maintaining control over how it accomplishes the task.

questions.question: A team wants to automate an insurance claims-intake process where the intake form, normalization, and routing are fixed, but the customer's free-text description is too varied to enumerate. Following the lesson's decision framework, how should they design it?
options: Make the whole system one fully autonomous agent, because any task that contains an unpredictable part must be entirely agentic
Route every step through the model at runtime so no design restriction is needed

Build a hybrid: orchestrate the enumerable steps (intake, normalize, route, validate, human approve) and give only the free-text analysis a bounded agent with a small tool palette, a step cap, and a schema its output is validated against
Skip automation entirely because the free text means no reliable system can be built
questions.explanation: The worked example is exactly this case. The enumerable steps are orchestrated predefined code, while the genuinely open-ended residue, parsing the free-text description, is the only step that gets a bounded agent with a small tool palette and a step cap. The expensive payment decision stays behind a human gate. Autonomy is used only where flexibility is worth the cost.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against giving autonomy to a whole task when only part of it is genuinely open-ended?
options: Because autonomous agents are always less accurate than workflows on every kind of task

Because autonomy trades latency and cost for flexibility, so every extra degree of model decision-making adds uncertainty about what the system will do, how long it will take, and how much it will spend, which is why you maximize determinism wherever the task allows
Because workflows never make mistakes, so adding agents always reduces correctness
Because models refuse to follow predefined steps, so any orchestration reduces their capability
questions.explanation: The lesson frames the choice as a tradeoff: moving toward autonomy buys capability and flexibility but at the cost of uncertainty about behavior, duration, and spend, and it requires earned trust. Anthropic's guidance is to find the simplest solution and only increase complexity when needed, maximizing determinism wherever the task allows and spending autonomy only on the genuinely open-ended residue.

questions.question: Per lesson 71, what is the load-bearing idea behind separating the control plane from the data plane in an agent platform?
options: The control plane and data plane must run on the same hardware so policy checks never add latency to the data path

The control plane governs and stays stable while the data plane executes and scales fast, and merging them makes each plane harder to operate because they change at different speeds and answer to different teams
The data plane is only needed for databases, so platforms without a database do not need one
The control plane is optional in small deployments, and only large enterprises need to separate the two
questions.explanation: The lesson states the separation is the load-bearing idea: the control plane decides and governs while the data plane executes. They are separate because they change at different speeds and answer to different teams. Merging them means every policy change risks the data path and every data-path change risks governance.

questions.question: A company's support agent reads case history and drafts a refund recommendation for human approval. Following the lesson's three-plane model, which plane decides that the refund draft requires additional checks and must be flagged for human approval?
options: The serving plane, because it selects which model handles the request
The data plane, because it controls which rows the agent can read
The control plane, because it enforces runtime policy and decides whether an action like a refund needs additional checks
The harness, because it owns the agent's memory and context window
questions.explanation: The worked example shows the control plane governs the action. When the agent tries to draft a refund, the control plane applies runtime policy: a refund requires additional checks, so the output is flagged for human approval rather than executed. The serving plane picks the model, the data plane carries the data, and the harness owns the loop.

questions.question: Why does the lesson argue that an agent platform's control plane should be portable and asset-aware rather than tied to a single cloud vendor's native governance?
options: Because native cloud governance is always slower than a custom-built control plane

Because governance expressed in native cloud constructs is non-transferable, so a multi-cloud portfolio needs separate governance stacks in different policy languages, and the tooling that appears free at signup becomes the lock-in mechanism at exit
Because cloud vendors do not offer any governance tooling for AI agents
Because asset-aware governance is required by law in every jurisdiction
questions.explanation: MuleSoft's argument, which the lesson adopts, is that native cloud governance is non-transferable: every policy and audit config is authored in a proprietary schema meaningful only inside that cloud. A multi-cloud portfolio needs separate stacks in different policy languages, and the free-looking tooling becomes lock-in at exit. An asset-aware control plane governs by what the asset is, not by who built it or which cloud it runs on.

questions.question: Per lesson 72, why is the gateway described as the load-bearing seam between the control plane and the data plane when building an agent platform?
options: Because it is the only component that can run large language models

Because it is the single point in the traffic path where policy can actually meet traffic and stop an action before it happens, so every request crosses it for authentication, routing, quotas, and logging
Because it stores all of the agent's long-term memory between sessions
Because it replaces the policy engine entirely, so no separate decision layer is needed
questions.explanation: The lesson states the gateway is the enforcement point that sits in the traffic path and intercepts every call before it reaches a model or tool. Policy written in a design document stops nothing; it only takes effect when it is enforced at the gateway, which authenticates the caller, applies rate limits and token budgets, routes the request, and writes the usage log.

questions.question: A support agent calls a refund-drafting tool and then tries to call an external payment tool directly. Using the lesson's PEP and PDP split, how does the system handle these two calls?
options: The data plane decides each call because it owns the rows the agent can read

The gateway authenticates the caller and asks the policy engine for an allow or deny decision; the default-deny Rego policy allows an agent to draft a refund but forbids an agent from invoking the external payment tool, so the second call is denied and logged
The serving plane picks a different model for each call based on cost
The refund draft is sent for human review while the payment call is always allowed because it needs to complete the refund
questions.explanation: The worked example shows the gateway acting as the policy enforcement point and the policy engine as the decision point. It posts a JSON input describing each tool call and asks for the value of allow. The policy starts from default allow := false, allows an agent to call the refund draft tool, and only allows the external payment tool for a human actor. The agent's second call returns false, so the gateway denies it and logs the action.

questions.question: Why does the lesson argue that a policy layer built with OPA or Cedar is safer to operate than policies expressed as scattered if statements inside application code?
options: Because OPA and Cedar are the only tools that support role-based access control

Because the policy becomes a separate, reviewable artifact that changes independently of application code, with default-deny as the default, and OPA handles policy versioning and rollback automatically through its management API

Because the policy is a separate artifact that changes independently of application code, it is versioned and reviewed in git as code, and a default-deny rule makes the safe path the default, though the organization still owns versioning and rollback because OPA does not manage policies by itself
Because OPA automatically fetches all external user data at request time inside the policy
questions.explanation: The lesson and the AWS prescriptive guidance it cites contrast the PEP and PDP split: the policy is a separate artifact (a Rego or Cedar file) that updates independently of the application, reviewed through pull requests and deployed by CI/CD. The guidance is explicit that OPA does not provide a control plane for managing policies by itself, so the company owns versioning and rollback. The safe path being the default comes from default-deny and forbid-wins semantics, which Cedar engines apply automatically.
